scope: One full authorized W4C guide plus one Original C transfer; no segmentation, processing, retry or canonical edit
text:
Most personalized books are one adventure with your kid's name dropped into it. Same story, different name.

But I wanted to make my son a book about what he was actually going through. He's obsessed with motorcycles. He calls them motos, that's just what they're called in our house now.

So I made him this. There's a moto named Mikey who has decided he'd rather be a car. Cars have roofs, cars have four wheels, cars get to go out in the rain. And then an actual car turns up, and she tells him she's wanted to be a moto her whole life.

They both want to be the thing the other one already is.

And that's the part I care about. There's no name slot for that.

So I make them for other people's kids now. You tell me what's going on for them right now, and who's actually in their life. Who does bedtime. Who coaches. And what you want it to look like. And I write the story around that. Then it gets printed once, for one child, and never printed again.

If you want one for your kid, message me.

input.prompt: Speak every supplied word exactly, in order, without adding, dropping, repeating or paraphrasing words. Keep every written contraction as one connected spoken word: kid's, he's, that's, they're, there's, he'd, she's and what's stay contracted, and do not expand any of them. Speak the three short consecutive sentences 'Who does bedtime. Who coaches. And what you want it to look like.' as three complete separate sentences, saying every one of them, with a small clear pause after each full stop. Speak to one capable peer at an ordinary conversational pace, as if they asked what you have been making lately. Use a close, comfortable, ordinarily projected voice. Be engaged, casual and matter-of-fact, telling it rather than reading it, with natural changes in emphasis and small pauses when the thought changes. Let pitch and phrase length vary with the meaning, without giving every sentence the same rise and fall or a punchline landing. The opening two sentences are a flat observation about how these books usually work, slightly dry, not a complaint and not a hook. 'But I wanted to make my son a book' is where it becomes personal; let it warm slightly without becoming sentimental. 'So I made him this' is said while holding the book up, so leave a small natural beat after it. Let the sentences about roofs and four wheels run lightly and quickly. Take a small pause before 'And then an actual car turns up' so the turn has room. Deliver 'They both want to be the thing the other one already is' plainly and without weight; it is an observation, not a moral. 'There's no name slot for that' is quiet and matter-of-fact, not a point being scored. The closing description of how the books are made is practical and unhurried. The final line 'If you want one for your kid, message me.' is ordinary and low-key, an offer rather than a pitch, with no rise in energy and no salesperson delivery. Land the final word and let it finish, followed by a small natural quiet ending. Do not imitate a narrator, presenter or motivational speaker. No imposed duration, accelerated target, exaggerated consonants, rehearsed stumbles, filler words, added breathing for effect, forced laughter, smile acting, music, ambience or effects. Do not speak these directions.
